rationale: #972. The analyzer's four name maps (structs, globalVars, unions, enums) are keyed by arbitrary C identifiers but were plain `{}`, so any lookup of an Object.prototype member name returned a truthy INHERITED value -- `structs['constructor']` is `Object`, `structs['toString']` is a function. `isResolvableUseTarget` ends in a plain truthiness test over all four, so such a name passed the resolvability gate and was published as a `uses` edge whether or not anything declared it. Measured at zig/lib/libc/mingw/winpthreads/thread.c:92, where the gcc attribute token `constructor` (declared nowhere) produced `uses ctor -> constructor` -- a dangling edge to a name with no symbol, the class #962 exists to remove. `constructor` is the rare name; `toString` and `valueOf` are ordinary C identifiers, so this is a live class. Fixed with Object.create(null) at the four DECLARATIONS rather than a guard at each of the 23 lookup sites, which also closes the write hazard: a struct named `__proto__` would otherwise assign the prototype instead of adding a key. The controls exist so that a fix which made the maps refuse to answer anything would FAIL this fixture rather than pass it.

expectRelationships.comment: CONTROL: a real call of a function whose name is an Object.prototype member. Call resolution reads the symbol table, not these maps, so it must be unaffected by #972.
CONTROL: an ordinary read of a file-scope variable. This edge depends on globalVars answering truthfully, so it is the direct inverse of the defect.

CONTROL: an assignment to a file-scope variable from inside a function whose HEADING carries a gcc attribute -- the corpus shape, with the attribute token now correctly ignored rather than the read beside it.

forbidRelationships.comment: THE defect #972 fixes. `constructor` is a gcc attribute token, declared nowhere, and resolved only because structs['constructor'] is Object.
Resolved only because the inherited member is truthy. There IS a function named toString here, so this row would have looked plausible -- which is why the controls above matter.
